title: Protective devices – co-ordination
summary: Explains co-ordination (discrimination) of protective devices, the fuse rating rule of thumb, the limit of discrimination, and S-Type RCDs.

sections.heading: What is co-ordination?
paragraphs: Co-ordination, which used to be called discrimination, is the co-ordination of two automatic circuit protective devices so that a fault at any given point in an installation is cleared by the protective device installed immediately upstream of the fault, and by that device alone.

In the example, a 100 A protective device feeds a 63 A sub-main that feeds a 30 A BS 3036 fuse in a distribution board. For a fault at the point shown, co-ordination occurs if only the 30 A device operates. There is a lack of co-ordination if either the 63 A or 100 A device operates.
bullets: Fault cleared by the device immediately upstream of the fault, and by that device alone
Example: 100 A feeds 63 A sub-main feeding a 30 A BS 3036 fuse
Only the 30 A device operating = co-ordination
63 A or 100 A operating = lack of co-ordination

sections.heading: Co-ordination between fuses
paragraphs: In simple terms, co-ordination is achieved for fuses if the upstream device rating is more than twice that of the downstream device. For example, with fuse A upstream at 80 A and fuse B downstream at 32 A, co-ordination is achieved because neither of the characteristics cross over.
The point at which the two time/current characteristics cross is called the limit of discrimination or selectivity.
bullets: Upstream rating more than twice the downstream rating
Example: 80 A upstream, 32 A downstream, characteristics do not cross
Crossing point of time/current characteristics = limit of discrimination or selectivity

sections.heading: RCDs and co-ordination
paragraphs: Where co-ordination is required between RCDs in series, the operating characteristics must be checked so that the required discrimination is provided. A correct design avoids nuisance tripping.

S-Type RCDs are designed to operate more slowly than standard RCDs, minimising the risk of nuisance tripping. In the example, the main switch is an S-Type RCD rated at 300 mA and a downstream device is a standard 30 mA RCD. Where S-Type RCDs are used, take care that the requirements of BS 7671 Regulations 411.3 and 411.5 are met.
bullets: Check operating characteristics of RCDs in series
S-Type RCDs operate more slowly than standard RCDs
Example: S-Type 300 mA main switch with standard 30 mA downstream
Ensure BS 7671 Regulations 411.3 and 411.5 are met

flashcards.front: What was co-ordination of protective devices previously called?

flashcards.back: A fault at any point is cleared by the protective device immediately upstream of the fault, and by that device alone.

flashcards.front: In the 100 A, 63 A and 30 A BS 3036 example, when is there co-ordination?
flashcards.back: If only the 30 A device operates.

flashcards.front: When is there a lack of co-ordination in that example?
flashcards.back: If the 63 A or the 100 A device operates.

flashcards.front: What simple rule achieves co-ordination for fuses?
flashcards.back: The upstream device rating is more than twice that of the downstream device.

flashcards.front: Why do an 80 A upstream fuse and 32 A downstream fuse co-ordinate?
flashcards.back: Neither of their characteristics cross over.

flashcards.front: What is the limit of discrimination?
flashcards.back: The point at which the two time/current characteristics cross; also called selectivity.

flashcards.front: How do S-Type RCDs help co-ordination?
flashcards.back: They operate more slowly than standard RCDs, minimising the risk of nuisance tripping.

flashcards.front: Which BS 7671 regulations must be met when S-Type RCDs are used?

quiz.q: What was co-ordination of protective devices formerly called?
quiz.why: Co-ordination used to be called discrimination.

quiz.q: Which device should clear a fault, if protective devices are co-ordinated?
options: The device immediately upstream of the fault, alone
All devices upstream of the fault
The device furthest from the fault
quiz.why: The fault is cleared by the device installed immediately upstream, and by that device alone.

quiz.q: A 100 A device feeds a 63 A sub-main feeding a 30 A BS 3036 fuse. For a fault on the 30 A circuit, which situation shows a lack of co-ordination?
quiz.why: A lack of co-ordination occurs if the 63 A or 100 A device operates.

quiz.q: For fuses, what rule of thumb achieves co-ordination?
options: Upstream rating more than twice the downstream rating
Upstream rating half the downstream rating
quiz.why: Co-ordination is achieved if the upstream rating is more than twice the downstream rating.

quiz.q: Fuse A (80 A) is upstream of fuse B (32 A). Why is co-ordination achieved?
options: Neither of their characteristics cross over
quiz.why: Co-ordination is achieved because neither characteristic crosses over.

quiz.q: What is the point where two time/current characteristics cross called?
options: The limit of discrimination or selectivity
quiz.why: It is called the limit of discrimination or selectivity.

quiz.q: How do S-Type RCDs differ from standard RCDs?
quiz.why: S-Type RCDs are designed to operate more slowly, minimising nuisance tripping.

quiz.q: In the RCD example, which pair is used?
options: S-Type 30 mA main, standard 300 mA downstream
Standard 300 mA main, S-Type 30 mA downstream
S-Type 300 mA main, standard 30 mA downstream
quiz.why: The main switch is an S-Type RCD rated at 300 mA with a standard 30 mA RCD downstream.
